```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE) &&
  utils::packageVersion("ggplot2") >= "3.4.0"
```

The README introduces LEARNER with one source and a common space penalty.
Here we extend that analysis in two directions: allowing different penalties
for the two latent spaces, and borrowing information from multiple sources.
We then check the selected parameters and the optimization results.

Paste each code block into the RStudio Console, or run it in an R script,
following the order below. The Copy buttons copy code
without the printed output; they do not run R in this page. The complete script
below uses the same examples and requires the package version accompanying this
vignette. Runtime depends on your machine and package build; the diagnostic section
repeats cross-validation (CV). To run the download, open `advanced-learner.R`
in RStudio and select Source with Echo, or run
`source("advanced-learner.R", echo = TRUE, max.deparse.length = Inf)` from
the directory where you saved it. Echo shows the code and printed results,
including selected penalties and stopping codes. Without `max.deparse.length`,
R may cut long echoed commands short with `[ TRUNCATED ]`; the printed
results are not affected.

```{r download-script, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
script_path <- "../inst/examples/advanced-learner.R"
if (!file.exists(script_path)) {
  script_path <- system.file("examples", "advanced-learner.R", package = "learner")
}
script_text <- paste(readLines(script_path, warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n")
cat('<p><a download="advanced-learner.R" href="data:text/plain;charset=utf-8,',
    utils::URLencode(script_text, reserved = TRUE),
    '">Download the complete R script</a></p>', sep = "")
```

### Before you start

This tutorial needs the development version of learner. Run the check below to
load the data and confirm that your installation supports the plotting calls.
If it fails, follow the installation instructions before continuing.

```{r load-package, message=FALSE}
install_help <- paste(
  "Install the development version of learner with",
  "devtools::install_github(\"stmcg/learner\"), then restart R and rerun",
  "from the top.")
if (!requireNamespace("learner", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop(install_help,
       call. = FALSE)
}
required_data <- c("dat_asymmetric", "dat_multisource")
available_data <- utils::data(package = "learner")$results[, "Item"]
missing_data <- setdiff(required_data, available_data)
if (length(missing_data)) {
  stop(paste0("Your installed learner package is missing: ",
              paste(missing_data, collapse = ", "),
              ". ", install_help), call. = FALSE)
}
library(learner)
data("dat_asymmetric", "dat_multisource", package = "learner")

if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE) ||
    utils::packageVersion("ggplot2") < "3.4.0") {
  stop('Install ggplot2 >= 3.4.0 with install.packages("ggplot2"), then rerun.',
       call. = FALSE)
}
# Check behavior rather than relying on a development version number.
compatible <- local({
  y <- diag(c(4, 2, 1))
  target <- diag(c(4, 0, 0))
  cv <- cv.learner(y, target, r = 1, lambda_1_all = 1, lambda_2_all = 1,
                   step_size = 0.001, n_folds = 2, control = list(max_iter = 2))
  all(c("lambda_1_all", "lambda_2_all", "n_observed") %in% names(cv))
})
if (!compatible) {
  stop(paste("This learner installation lacks the CV metadata used here.",
             install_help), call. = FALSE)
}

```

If this block reports errors, resolve the first error before running anything
else. Pasting several expressions into the Console can continue after an error;
later messages may only be consequences of the first failure.

### Installation

This tutorial needs the development version of learner. The version on CRAN
(1.0.0 at the time of writing) does not include the example datasets or the
plotting functions used here. Install the development version from GitHub:

```
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("stmcg/learner")
```

Restart R after installing, then run the first code block again. The package
compiles C++ code, so you need a compiler: Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS or
Rtools on Windows.

If the check still fails after installing, use `packageVersion("learner")` and
`find.package("learner")` to see which installation R is using.



An OpenMP startup message means that multithreading is unavailable in that
installation. These examples use the default single core and can still run.

## 1. Base Case: D-LEARNER and LEARNER with One Source

Write the target estimate as $UV^\top$, with $U$ of size $p\times r$ and $V$
of size $q\times r$. Let $P_U$ and $P_V$ project onto the leading source
singular-vector spaces. The columns of $U$ span the signal matrix's column
space, and the columns of $V$ span its row space. We use U-space and
V-space throughout. In the package interface, `lambda_1_row` acts on $U$
and `lambda_1_col` acts on $V$.

D-LEARNER estimates the target by direct projection, $P_UY_0P_V$, without
iterative optimization or penalty tuning. LEARNER fits target factors while
penalizing departures from the source spaces. With complete target data $Y_0$,
its single-source, common-penalty objective is

$$
L(U,V)=\|UV^\top-Y_0\|_F^2
+\lambda_1\|(I_p-P_U)U\|_F^2
+\lambda_1\|(I_q-P_V)V\|_F^2
+\lambda_2\|U^\top U-V^\top V\|_F^2.
$$

The first term fits the target data. The next two encourage the target factors
to follow the source spaces, with common strength `lambda_1`. The last term,
controlled by `lambda_2`, balances the scales of the two factors.

For missing target entries, the fit term uses only observed entries and is
divided by the observed fraction. Penalty terms stay the same. The examples
below have complete observed matrices and fix the rank at 3 to focus on the
extensions. See `?learner` for optimization settings and stopping codes.

## 2. Separate U- and V-Space Penalties

### An asymmetric example

`dat_asymmetric` contains one source and one target, each with 100 rows and 50
columns. Their rank-3 true signals share the U-space but have different
V-spaces. Independent normal noise has variance 0.10 for the target and 0.01
for the source. The estimated spaces are affected by noise, even on the shared
side.

The construction follows the U-shared/V-perturbed setting in Section 2.4.1 of
the Supporting Information of McGrath et al. (2026), with smaller matrices and
rank 3. See `?dat_asymmetric` for details. The dataset includes the true signals,
but the fitting and tuning code below uses only the observed matrices.

```{r asymmetric-data}
asym <- dat_asymmetric
```

### Specify separate penalties

A source may resemble the target more closely in one space than in the other.
Separate penalties let us control how strongly LEARNER borrows from each:

$$
L_{\rm separate}(U,V)=\|UV^\top-Y_0\|_F^2
+\lambda_{1,\rm row}\|(I_p-P_U)U\|_F^2
+\lambda_{1,\rm col}\|(I_q-P_V)V\|_F^2
+\lambda_2\|U^\top U-V^\top V\|_F^2.
$$

Use `lambda_1_row` for U and `lambda_1_col` for V. Equal values recover the
common-penalty objective. Larger values impose stronger constraints; the
penalties are not direct measurements of similarity. D-LEARNER has no penalty
parameters, so this extension applies to LEARNER.

### Select penalties and refit

Supply both space grids to `cv.learner()` instead of `lambda_1_all`. It evaluates
all row, column, and balance combinations. Calling `set.seed()` makes the random
fold assignment reproducible.

The default stopping rule checks whether the absolute change between successive
recorded objective values is below `0.001`. We raise the iteration limit from
100 to 2000 for both CV and the final fit, giving each fit more time to meet
that threshold. Fits can stop earlier. The step size is `0.003`; Section 4
checks how the results change with a smaller step and a larger iteration limit.

```{r asymmetric-cv}
asym_space_grid <- c(0, 10, 100)
asym_balance_grid <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
set.seed(815)
cv_separate <- cv.learner(
  asym$Y_source, asym$Y_target, r = 3,
  lambda_1_row_all = asym_space_grid,
  lambda_1_col_all = asym_space_grid,
  lambda_2_all = asym_balance_grid,
  n_folds = 3, step_size = 0.003, control = list(max_iter = 2000))
c(U = cv_separate$lambda_1_row_min,
  V = cv_separate$lambda_1_col_min,
  balance = cv_separate$lambda_2_min)
```

Use the selected penalties to refit with all observed target entries:

```{r asymmetric-refit}
fit_separate <- learner(
  asym$Y_source, asym$Y_target, r = cv_separate$r,
  lambda_1_row = cv_separate$lambda_1_row_min,
  lambda_1_col = cv_separate$lambda_1_col_min,
  lambda_2 = cv_separate$lambda_2_min,
  step_size = 0.003, control = list(max_iter = 2000))
dim(fit_separate$learner_estimate)
fit_separate$convergence_criterion
```

`learner_estimate` contains the fitted target matrix. The stopping code applies
to this final fit: 1 means the stopping criterion was met, 2 means the iteration
limit was reached, and 3 indicates excessive objective growth or non-finite
values. Section 4 checks the fits within CV separately.

### View the CV results

`plot_cv()` reads the grids and observed-entry count from the CV result.
It uses ggplot2, which we checked at the start.

```{r asymmetric-cv-plot, eval=has_ggplot, fig.alt="CV errors across U and V penalties, with one panel per balance penalty and a black outline marking the selected candidate."}
plot_cv(cv_separate)
```

Each panel corresponds to one balance penalty. The axes show the U and V
penalties, and the black outline marks the selected combination. Pale blue
indicates lower error; dark blue indicates higher error, on the same scale
across panels. Cell labels give the percentage increase above the minimum CV
mean squared error (MSE). Values are rounded, so a label of zero does not
necessarily mean an exact tie. Gray cells, when present, mark unavailable
scores or scores above the plotting cutoff.

## 3. Multiple Sources and Source Weights

### Prepare aligned sources

`dat_multisource` contains one target and two sources, each with 100 rows and 50
columns. Their rank-3 true signals share latent spaces. Independent normal
noise has variance 0.10 for the target, 0.01 for A, and 0.50 for B, so A is
observed more precisely than B.

```{r multiple-data}
sources <- dat_multisource$Y_source
target <- dat_multisource$Y_target
weights <- c(0.7, 0.3)
```

Supply sources as a list of matrices, with rows and columns in the same order
as the target. The functions do not align them for you. Weights follow the list
order and are normalized to sum to one; omitting them gives equal weights.
Here we choose 0.7 for A and 0.3 for B as an example. CV does not select these
weights.

### Combine source-space information

For source $k$, let $\hat U_k$ and $\hat V_k$ contain its leading orthonormal
singular vectors at the chosen rank. Both methods use

$$
\bar P_U=\sum_k w_k\hat U_k\hat U_k^\top,\qquad
\bar P_V=\sum_k w_k\hat V_k\hat V_k^\top,
\quad w_k\geq0,\quad\sum_k w_k=1.
$$

The same source weights apply to both sides. These are weighted combinations
of projection matrices, not averages of the observed source matrices. The
combined matrices need not themselves be orthogonal projectors. A larger weight
gives a source more influence, but does not guarantee greater accuracy.

### Fit D-LEARNER

D-LEARNER uses the combined matrices directly:

$$
\widehat\Theta_{\rm D}=\bar P_UY_0\bar P_V.
$$

```{r multiple-direct}
fit_direct <- dlearner(sources, target, r = 3, source_weights = weights)
dim(fit_direct$dlearner_estimate)
```

The result is stored in `dlearner_estimate`. No step size, iterative optimization,
or penalty selection is needed. Combining both sides in this way is generally
not the same as averaging separately fitted single-source estimates.

### Select penalties and fit LEARNER

LEARNER uses the same combined matrices in its space penalties. With a common
space penalty, the objective is

$$
L_{\rm multi}(U,V)=\|UV^\top-Y_0\|_F^2
+\lambda_1\|(I_p-\bar P_U)U\|_F^2
+\lambda_1\|(I_q-\bar P_V)V\|_F^2
+\lambda_2\|U^\top U-V^\top V\|_F^2.
$$

Source weights determine each source's contribution to the combined matrices;
the penalties determine how strongly the target factors are constrained by
them. LEARNER initializes from the first source and also uses that source to
choose the rank when `r` is omitted.

We keep the weights fixed during CV and use a step size of `0.0003` for this
example.

```{r multiple-cv}
set.seed(815)
cv_multi <- cv.learner(
  sources, target, r = 3, source_weights = weights,
  lambda_1_all = c(0, 1, 10), lambda_2_all = c(0.1, 1),
  n_folds = 3, step_size = 0.0003, control = list(max_iter = 2000))
c(space = cv_multi$lambda_1_min, balance = cv_multi$lambda_2_min)
```

```{r multiple-cv-plot, eval=has_ggplot, fig.alt="Multiple-source CV error heatmap; the selected candidate lies at the upper endpoints of both grids."}
plot_cv(cv_multi)
```

The axes now show the common space penalty and the balance penalty. Both
selected values, 10 and 1, are the largest in their grids, hence the caption
"Selection on grid boundary". These small grids keep the example short; an
analysis using these data should check a wider range.

Of the 18 internal CV fits, 4 reach the 2000-update limit, including 2 of the
3 folds for the selected candidate. Their final objective values alternate
between higher and lower values. A successful final fit therefore does not
establish that all CV fits met the stopping criterion. Check the step size as
well as the iteration limit when you see this pattern.

Refit with the same weights and the selected penalties:

```{r multiple-refit}
fit_multi <- learner(
  sources, target, r = cv_multi$r, source_weights = weights,
  lambda_1 = cv_multi$lambda_1_min, lambda_2 = cv_multi$lambda_2_min,
  step_size = 0.0003, control = list(max_iter = 2000))
dim(fit_multi$learner_estimate)
fit_multi$convergence_criterion
```

Multiple sources can also be combined with separate penalties: replace
`lambda_1_all` in the CV call by both separate grids, and refit with the selected
`lambda_1_row` and `lambda_1_col` as in Section 2. Source weights stay fixed in
both workflows; selecting weights by CV is outside this tutorial.

## 4. Diagnostics and Sensitivity Checks

Run Section 2 through the final refit before starting these checks. They use
`asym`, `asym_space_grid`, `asym_balance_grid`, `cv_separate`, and `fit_separate`
from that section. Section 3 is not needed.

### Check grid boundaries and similar CV scores

First, compare the selected penalties with the ends of their candidate grids:

```{r grid-boundaries}
needed <- c("asym", "asym_space_grid", "asym_balance_grid",
            "cv_separate", "fit_separate")
if (!all(vapply(needed, exists, logical(1), inherits = TRUE))) {
  stop("Run Section 2 through the final refit before starting Section 4.",
       call. = FALSE)
}
selected <- c(U = cv_separate$lambda_1_row_min,
              V = cv_separate$lambda_1_col_min,
              balance = cv_separate$lambda_2_min)
grids <- list(cv_separate$lambda_1_row_all, cv_separate$lambda_1_col_all,
              cv_separate$lambda_2_all)
data.frame(parameter = names(selected), selected = unname(selected),
           lower = vapply(grids, min, numeric(1)),
           upper = vapply(grids, max, numeric(1)),
           on_boundary = vapply(seq_along(grids), function(i) {
             selected[i] %in% range(grids[[i]])
           }, logical(1)))
```

The selected U penalty is at the upper end of its grid, as the heatmap caption
also notes. Try extending that grid while keeping the data and fold seed fixed.

When several CV scores are close, a small change in the folds or optimization
settings may change which candidate is selected. In that case, avoid attaching
too much importance to a single selected value. Also remember that the minimum
CV score was used for tuning; it is not an independent test error.

### Inspect the objective history

```{r asymmetric-objective, fig.alt="Objective values near the smallest recorded value, at the final update of a fit stopped by the tolerance criterion."}
plot_objective(fit_separate, iterations = "near_optimum")
```

The plot shows up to 41 recorded values near the minimum. Here the minimum is
at the last recorded update, so it appears at the right edge of the window.
The curve still slopes down, but the final change is below the tolerance:
the fit stopped at update 700 with code 1, before reaching the 2000-update limit.

Use `iterations = "all"` to see the full history, or `iterations = 1:100` to
choose a range. If a fit reaches its limit with code 2 while the objective is
still decreasing, allow more updates. If successive values oscillate, try a
different step size. Neither a flat-looking curve nor code 1 establishes a
global minimum.

### Repeat CV with a few optimization settings

We compare the original settings with two alternatives: a larger iteration
limit, and a smaller step size with that larger limit. The data, rank, grids,
and CV folds stay fixed, so the comparison isolates the optimization settings.

```{r sensitivity-checks}
fit_summary <- function(cv, fit, step, budget) {
  data.frame(step_size = step, max_iter = budget,
             U = cv$lambda_1_row_min, V = cv$lambda_1_col_min,
             balance = cv$lambda_2_min,
             min_cv_mse = min(cv$mse_all) / cv$n_observed,
             updates = length(fit$objective_values),
             stop_code = fit$convergence_criterion)
}
check_setting <- function(step, budget) {
  set.seed(815)
  cv <- cv.learner(
    asym$Y_source, asym$Y_target, r = 3,
    lambda_1_row_all = asym_space_grid,
    lambda_1_col_all = asym_space_grid, lambda_2_all = asym_balance_grid,
    n_folds = 3, step_size = step, control = list(max_iter = budget))
  fit <- learner(
    asym$Y_source, asym$Y_target, r = cv$r,
    lambda_1_row = cv$lambda_1_row_min, lambda_1_col = cv$lambda_1_col_min,
    lambda_2 = cv$lambda_2_min, step_size = step,
    control = list(max_iter = budget))
  fit_summary(cv, fit, step, budget)
}
sensitivity <- rbind(
  fit_summary(cv_separate, fit_separate, 0.003, 2000),
  check_setting(0.003, 4000),
  check_setting(0.0015, 4000))
print(sensitivity, row.names = FALSE)
```

Increasing the iteration limit leaves the selected penalties and CV score
unchanged, and the final fit still stops at update 700. With the smaller step,
the final fit takes 1352 updates; the selected penalties are the same and the
CV MSE is close to the original value.

These three settings give a useful first check. For your own data, extend the
comparison if the selected penalties or scores change substantially. The final
stopping codes do not tell us how every fit inside CV ended.

### Inspect the CV fits for the selected candidate

`cv.learner()` does not return the internal stopping codes. We can inspect the
selected candidate by recreating the three folds with the same seed and fitting
each training set again:

```{r inner-cv-stopping}
set.seed(815)
indices <- sample(which(!is.na(asym$Y_target)))
n <- length(indices)
folds <- lapply(1:3, function(k) {
  indices[seq.int(floor((k - 1) * n / 3) + 1, floor(k * n / 3))]
})
inner_fits <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(k) {
  training <- asym$Y_target
  training[folds[[k]]] <- NA
  fit <- learner(
    asym$Y_source, training, r = cv_separate$r,
    lambda_1_row = cv_separate$lambda_1_row_min,
    lambda_1_col = cv_separate$lambda_1_col_min,
    lambda_2 = cv_separate$lambda_2_min,
    step_size = 0.003, control = list(max_iter = 2000))
  data.frame(fold = k, updates = length(fit$objective_values),
             stop_code = fit$convergence_criterion)
}))
print(inner_fits, row.names = FALSE)
```

All three fits meet the stopping criterion here. This check covers the selected
candidate only; checking the whole search would require repeating it for each
combination in the grids. If any fit reaches its iteration limit, inspect its
objective history and try a different budget or step size before relying on
the selection.
